vignette: Thomas, a 72-year-old software engineer who lives alone in a modest house in the suburbs, began his journey toward this session after a lifetime of quiet torment that started at the age of 27 during a brief, brutal period of captivity on a distant war-zone base. The torture he endured was not a single moment but a succession of daily abuses-his hands were bound for hours, he was struck with a metal rod while lying on the floor, and his voice was silenced with a gag that made it feel as if his very self had been broken. Those days left a scar that Thomas would carry for decades. He remembers the feeling of his chest tightening, his breath caught as if the world itself was collapsing. When he later thought about what had happened, he felt his moral compass turned inward; he began to believe that he had acted in ways that were not at all in line with the integrity he had always carried-an appraisement he would label "violated values." That sense of having betrayed his own core identity seeped into his everyday life, and with it, a gnawing fear that he might slip again into that loss of self. Because of this, Thomas constantly monitors his own thoughts, convinced that any slip might signal a return to that helplessness, or that he is "going crazy." He tells his therapist that he scans himself, searching for the slightest aberration-an anxious tremor, a fleeting thought of violence, a sudden urge to scream-any sign that the past might intrude. The same fear drives him to suppress any recollection of the abuse. When the image of the metal rod surfaces, he will abruptly close his eyes or turn the conversation to his codebase, refusing to let the memory linger. His avoidance of solitude-never staying alone in a room or building-is a desperate effort to keep the past at bay; the isolation he experiences in a quiet office feels like the torture itself. Thomas's own appraisal that he has violated his values feeds directly into these strategies: the more he feels he has lost his core, the more he clings to the illusion that the thought-monitoring, suppression, and avoidance are shields against becoming that "other self" again. In turn, the continual vigilance and suppression only deepen his conviction that he has indeed betrayed his nature, reinforcing the negative appraisal he carries. At the same time, Thomas is acutely aware of any threat in his environment. He has learned to read faces and body language, watching for a flicker of malice even in a friendly coworker's smile. He repeatedly checks that doors and windows are locked, even after he has been in the same house for years, because a sudden creak reminds him of the sound of a hand on a door in the basement during his captivity. At night, his insomnia is not merely a lack of sleep; it is a constant alertness, a state of hyper-vigilance that keeps his mind on the possible return of danger. Thomas says that this sense of threat makes him feel that the world is untrustworthy, that every stranger, every creak, and every silence could hide a threat. The persistent perception of danger pushes him toward the same maladaptive tactics-thought monitoring, suppression, avoidance-because these are the only strategies he believes can keep the threat at bay. The threat also sharpens his negative appraisals: he feels that he has lost faith in people, in life, and in any higher power that might provide safety. That loss of faith only makes him more suspicious of others, more likely to read hostile intent in faces, and more likely to lock his doors repeatedly, which feeds back into his sense of ongoing danger. Now, after years of living with these patterns, Thomas's work has begun to suffer. In the last three months, he has missed deadlines because he spends hours re-checking code, doubting whether it might contain a flaw that could "trigger" a failure. His colleagues remark that he seems distracted, often looking over his shoulder at the screen as if a hidden threat might emerge. The isolation he feels-both self-imposed and imposed by others-has grown; he avoids company lunch meetings and chooses to work from home, where he can lock the door behind him and monitor the faces of his coworkers only through video. The cumulative burden of constant vigilance and avoidance has made the prospect of continuing alone unbearable. Finally, the loss of sleep, the endless anxiety, and the growing sense that he is no longer the person he once was have pushed him to seek help. He is most afraid that the strategies he has adopted are only perpetuating a cycle of self-doubt and isolation, yet he hopes that by confronting the memories and learning new coping tools, he might regain the faith he once had in people, in himself, and in a world that does not require him to live in perpetual threat.
